title: Should students have homework on weekends?
description: Should schools assign homework on weekends, or should those days stay free for rest and family time?
summary:
Weekend homework can help students remember what they learned during the week. A short reading or a few practice questions may make Monday’s lesson easier. Some students also like finishing work at their own pace instead of rushing through it after school. Teachers can use homework to see which ideas need more explanation.

However, weekends are important for sleep, sports, hobbies, chores and time with family. Students who have many assignments may feel that school never stops. Some families also have limited internet access or share one quiet place to study, so the same task can be much harder for them.

A middle plan could be to avoid required weekend work except for longer projects that students can plan ahead. Schools might also set a maximum amount of homework for the whole week. Would a homework-free weekend help students learn better, or would a small amount of practice be useful? What rule would feel fair to students with different schedules?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should students have homework on weekends?

title: Should schools require uniforms?
description: Do uniforms make school fairer and simpler, or should students choose their own clothes?
summary:
Some people support school uniforms because they make mornings easier. Students do not need to spend as much time choosing clothes, and families may find it simpler to buy a small set of school outfits. Uniforms can also make students feel that they belong to one community. Supporters say they reduce pressure to wear expensive brands.

Other students want to choose their own clothes. Clothing can show a person’s style, culture or interests, and a uniform may feel uncomfortable or too strict. Uniforms also cost money, especially when schools require special items from one shop. Even when everyone wears the same clothes, students may still compare shoes, bags or phones.

Schools could offer a few acceptable choices, such as different colors or styles, and provide help for families who need it. They could also ask students what feels comfortable and practical. Should schools choose one uniform for everyone, allow a simple dress code, or let students decide? Which choice would be fairest?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should schools require uniforms?

title: Should students keep phones in class?
description: Should students be allowed to use phones during lessons for learning and quick communication?
summary:
Phones can support learning when teachers plan how to use them. Students may look up a word, photograph homework instructions or answer a quick class poll. A phone can also help a student contact family after school. If a lesson uses a map, timer or language app, one device may make the activity easier.

Phones can also interrupt learning. Messages, games and videos compete for attention, even when students mean to focus. A phone on a desk may distract nearby classmates too. Not every student has the same device or data plan, so a phone-based activity can leave some people out. Teachers may spend time solving technical problems instead of teaching.

One option is to keep phones away unless a teacher asks the class to use them. Another is to allow phones for specific learning tasks and set clear rules for other times. Schools can provide shared devices when possible. Should students keep phones in their bags, use them only with permission, or have more freedom? What rule would help everyone learn?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should students keep phones in class?

title: Should the school day start later?
description: Would a later first lesson help students feel rested, or make the rest of the day harder to manage?
summary:
A later school start could give teenagers more time to sleep. Students who arrive tired may find it difficult to listen, remember new information or stay patient with classmates. A calmer morning could also make the trip to school safer for students who currently leave home before sunrise. Supporters say a schedule should match the needs of the people learning in it.

Changing the start time can create problems for families. Parents may need to begin work early, and younger children might still attend school at the usual time. Sports, music lessons and part-time jobs could finish later in the evening. Bus routes may also need to change, which can be expensive and complicated.

A school could try a later start for one term and ask students, families and staff how it affects sleep, travel and activities. It might also adjust the length of lunch or after-school programs. Should schools begin later, keep their current schedules, or test a change first? Which people should have a voice in the decision?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should the school day start later?

title: Should students use AI study tools?
description: Can AI help students learn and revise, or can it make it too easy to avoid doing the thinking themselves?
summary:
AI study tools can explain a difficult idea in simpler words, suggest practice questions or help students organize notes. A learner can ask for another example when a textbook explanation does not make sense. Used carefully, these tools may help students practice at their own speed and prepare better questions for a teacher.

There are risks too. A tool can give a wrong answer in a confident voice, and students may not notice the mistake. If someone asks AI to write an entire assignment, the student may finish quickly but learn very little. Some tools collect information, so students need to know what happens to their work and personal details.

Schools could teach students to check AI answers against trusted lessons and to explain their own reasoning. Teachers might allow AI for brainstorming but require students to show drafts or discuss their choices. Should students be allowed to use AI for schoolwork? Which tasks are helpful uses, and which tasks should remain the student’s responsibility?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should students use AI study tools?

title: Are zoos good for animals?
description: Do zoos protect animals and teach visitors, or should wild animals live only in natural habitats?
summary:
Some zoos care for animals that need help and support breeding programs for species at risk. Visitors can see animals closely and learn why habitats matter. A zoo may also help people feel connected to wildlife they would never meet in the wild. These experiences can encourage support for conservation work.

Critics argue that even a well-managed enclosure cannot offer the space and choices an animal has in its natural habitat. Some animals may feel stress when visitors watch them all day. They also ask whether money spent on zoos would do more good if it protected forests, oceans and wildlife in the wild. The quality of care can differ between places.

A useful discussion can compare different kinds of animal care, not just ask whether every zoo is the same. Students might look at enclosure size, enrichment, rescue work and conservation goals. Are zoos helpful places for animals and people, or should society focus on wildlife protection outside zoos? What evidence would you want before deciding?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Are zoos good for animals?

title: Should every neighborhood have a community garden?
description: Would a shared garden improve neighborhood life, or would it be difficult to maintain fairly?
summary:
A community garden gives neighbors a place to grow vegetables, herbs and flowers together. People can learn how plants grow and share fresh food. A garden can turn an unused space into somewhere pleasant to meet. Children may enjoy caring for a small plot, while older residents can share gardening skills with others.

A garden needs land, water, tools and regular care. If only a few people do the work, they may feel tired or resentful. Some neighborhoods have little open space, and not every resident wants to garden. Organizers also need clear rules about who can use the harvest and how to handle broken tools or empty plots.

A small pilot garden could help a neighborhood see what works. The group might choose a few shared crops, make a watering schedule and set aside some food for anyone who needs it. Should local governments or residents create more community gardens? How could a garden welcome people who have different amounts of time and experience?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should every neighborhood have a community garden?

title: Should public transport be free for students?
description: Would free buses and trains help students reach school and activities, or would another discount be enough?
summary:
Free public transport could make it easier for students to get to school, sports and clubs. Families would save money, and students might have more independence if they could travel safely without asking for a ride. If more people used buses and trains, roads could also feel less crowded during busy times.

Transport still costs money to run. If students do not pay fares, a city must find that money elsewhere or reduce other services. Some students live far from a bus route, so a free pass would not solve their travel problem. Crowded vehicles may also need more staff or more frequent trips.

A city could start with free travel during school hours or offer a student pass at a reduced price. It could ask students which routes they use and whether transport feels safe and reliable. Should students ride for free, receive a discount, or get help only when their families need it? What information would help a community choose?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should public transport be free for students?

title: Should schools stop selling bottled water?
description: Would refill stations reduce waste, or do students need bottled water as a convenient backup?
summary:
Schools can reduce waste by encouraging students to bring reusable water bottles. Refill stations make it easy to use the same bottle throughout the day, and students may avoid buying a new plastic bottle each time they feel thirsty. A school could give new students a bottle and explain how to clean it safely.

Some people rely on bottled water because they forget their bottle, lose it or do not have one at home. Refill stations can break, and students need clean water that tastes safe. If a school removes every bottled option before a good refill system exists, students may have fewer choices.

A fair plan could add refill stations first, keep a small backup supply and offer low-cost reusable bottles. Students could help check whether the stations are working. Should schools stop selling bottled water, or should they focus on making refills easy before changing sales? What would make the plan practical for everyone?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should schools stop selling bottled water?

title: Are team sports better than individual sports?
description: Do team sports teach more useful skills, or can individual sports offer students stronger personal goals?
summary:
Team sports can teach players to communicate, cooperate and trust one another. A team shares wins and losses, so students learn that success often depends on many people doing their part. Practices can also help classmates meet friends outside their usual groups. For some students, belonging to a team makes exercise more enjoyable.

Individual sports can build focus and self-discipline. A runner or swimmer can set personal goals and see progress without comparing every result to a team score. Students may also find more flexible ways to practice, especially if they cannot attend a team’s regular schedule. Individual sports still involve coaches, training partners and supporters.

Different students enjoy different kinds of challenge. Schools can offer both team and individual activities when space and staff allow. Should a school spend more money on team sports or individual sports? What matters most: cooperation, personal progress, competition, health or access for beginners?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Are team sports better than individual sports?

title: Should school cafeterias offer a vegetarian day?
description: Would a weekly vegetarian menu be a good way to add choice and reduce the school’s impact, or should every student choose daily?
summary:
A vegetarian menu day could introduce students to meals made with beans, lentils, vegetables and grains. These foods can be tasty and filling when the menu is planned well. Offering a meat-free day may also help a school use fewer ingredients with a large environmental footprint. Students could learn about food traditions from different cultures.

Some students may dislike the menu or worry that it will not keep them full. Others have allergies, health needs or family food traditions that the school should respect. A poorly planned menu might leave students with few choices, even if the goal is positive.

A cafeteria could ask students to taste several meals before choosing a weekly menu. It could keep an alternative available and clearly label ingredients. Should schools have one vegetarian day each week, offer vegetarian meals every day, or let students choose from a balanced menu? How can a school respect different needs while encouraging students to try new foods?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should school cafeterias offer a vegetarian day?

title: Should classrooms have pets?
description: Can caring for a classroom animal teach responsibility, or is a pet’s welfare too difficult to manage at school?
summary:
A classroom pet can help students learn about animal needs and routines. Students may enjoy observing how an animal eats, moves and rests. A shared care schedule can teach responsibility, and a pet may make the room feel welcoming. Teachers can connect daily care to science lessons about living things.

Animals need attention every day, including weekends and school holidays. A classroom may be noisy or stressful for some pets. Students can have allergies or feel afraid, and the school must make sure the animal is handled safely. If no adult can take responsibility, the pet may not receive consistent care.

A school should consider the animal’s needs before its own excitement. It might invite a trained guest to teach about animals instead, or choose a classroom project that does not involve keeping a pet. Should classrooms have animals, or are other ways of learning safer and kinder? What questions must a school answer before bringing any animal into a classroom?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should classrooms have pets?

title: Should students choose more of their school subjects?
description: Would more choice make learning more motivating, or should schools set a common program for everyone?
summary:
When students choose some subjects, they can spend time on interests and strengths. A student who enjoys art, technology or languages may work harder when the timetable includes those subjects. Choice can also help students explore possible careers and feel more responsible for their learning.

A common program ensures that everyone studies important skills. Students may not yet know which subjects they will need later, so a choice made early could close useful options. Schools also have limited teachers and rooms. If many students choose the same popular class, the school may not be able to offer it to everyone.

One plan is to keep a shared set of core subjects while allowing choices for part of the week. Schools could ask students to review their choices each term and explain what each course helps them learn. Should teenagers choose more classes, or should schools decide most subjects for them? Which skills should every student study together?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should students choose more of their school subjects?

title: Are digital books better than printed books for school?
description: Should schools use more e-books for convenience, or keep printed books as the main option?
summary:
Digital books are easy to carry and can include search tools, audio or adjustable text size. A student can keep several books on one device and look up a word quickly. Schools may also update digital materials without printing a new copy for every class. For some learners, a screen reader makes reading more accessible.

Printed books do not need a battery or internet connection. Some students find it easier to focus on paper, and they can write notes in the margins. A screen may bring notifications and other distractions. Devices also cost money, can break and may not be equally available to every student.

Schools could offer both formats and let students choose when possible. They might use printed books for longer reading and digital copies for quick reference. Are e-books better for learning, or do printed books still have an important place? Which format helps you concentrate, remember ideas and access the text?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Are digital books better than printed books for school?

title: Should students have longer breaks during the school day?
description: Would longer breaks help students return to class ready to learn, or make the school day too long?
summary:
Longer breaks give students time to eat slowly, move around and talk with friends. A short walk or game can help people return to class with more energy. Students who need extra time to reach the cafeteria or use the bathroom may feel less rushed. Breaks can also help classmates build friendships.

Longer breaks can make the school day end later. Families may have work schedules, and students may need time for sports, jobs or caring for siblings. A longer break is not helpful if there is nowhere comfortable to go or if students must wait in a crowded area. Teachers also need enough time to cover lessons.

A school might add a few minutes to lunch or create short movement breaks between difficult lessons. It can ask students where the schedule feels rushed. Should schools make breaks longer, keep them as they are, or add more short breaks? What kind of break helps students return to learning?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should students have longer breaks during the school day?

title: Should every student complete volunteer hours?
description: Would required volunteering help students contribute to their community, or should service stay a personal choice?
summary:
Volunteer work can connect students with people and places outside school. Helping at a library, park or community event may teach practical skills and show how local groups solve problems. Students can discover interests they did not know they had. A shared service project can also bring classmates together around a useful goal.

A requirement can feel unfair if students have family responsibilities, paid work or health needs. Some communities have fewer volunteer opportunities nearby, and transport can be a barrier. If students only work to collect hours, they may not feel personally connected to the service. Community groups need volunteers who are prepared, not simply present.

Schools could offer several ways to contribute and allow students to complete service during the school day. They could recognize caring actions without turning every act into a score. Should volunteer hours be required for graduation, encouraged but optional, or built into class projects? How can a school make service accessible and meaningful?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should every student complete volunteer hours?

title: Are group projects a fair way to grade students?
description: Do group projects teach cooperation, or can one shared grade hide differences in effort?
summary:
Group projects let students practice planning, explaining ideas and solving disagreements. A team can produce something more creative than one person could make alone. Students may also learn from classmates who have different strengths. In many jobs, people need to share tasks, so group work can provide useful practice.

A shared grade can be frustrating when some students do much more work than others. Confident speakers may lead every decision, while quieter students contribute less visibly. A group can also lose time if members cannot agree or if one person misses meetings. A good project needs clear roles and a fair way to notice each student’s learning.

Teachers can combine a group score with a short individual reflection, peer feedback or a personal task. Students can agree on roles before work begins and check progress together. Are group projects fair? What should count in a grade: the final product, each person’s contribution, teamwork, or all three?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Are group projects a fair way to grade students?

title: Should cities plant more trees along streets?
description: Can street trees make neighborhoods healthier and more pleasant, or do they create costs and maintenance problems?
summary:
Street trees can give shade on hot days and make a walk feel more pleasant. Trees provide places for birds and insects, and they can make a neighborhood greener. A row of trees may also encourage people to walk instead of driving short distances. Residents often enjoy streets that feel welcoming and cared for.

Trees need space, water and regular maintenance. Roots can damage sidewalks or pipes if the wrong species is planted in the wrong place. Fallen leaves need to be cleared, and young trees may not survive without care. Some streets have narrow sidewalks or underground services that limit where trees can grow.

Cities can choose suitable native trees, plant them with community input and plan who will care for them. They can start with a few blocks and learn from the results. Should cities plant more street trees? Which places should come first, and how can residents help keep the trees healthy?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should cities plant more trees along streets?

title: Should social media have a higher minimum age?
description: Would a higher age limit protect young people online, or should families and schools focus on safer use?
summary:
A higher minimum age for social media could give younger children more time to build confidence before facing online pressure. Some platforms show upsetting material or encourage people to compare themselves with carefully edited images. A clear age rule may also remind companies that young users need strong privacy and safety protections.

Age limits are difficult to enforce. Children may use a family member’s account or enter a false birthday. Social media can also help young people stay in touch with friends, share creative work and find supportive groups. A strict rule may remove those benefits without teaching students how to make safe choices.

Families, schools and technology companies can all help by teaching privacy, kindness and screen balance. Platforms could offer safer settings by default and make it easy to report harmful content. Should the minimum age be raised, kept the same, or supported by stronger safety rules? What responsibility should belong to the platform?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should social media have a higher minimum age?

title: Should schools spend more money on clubs than sports?
description: How should schools divide limited funds between sports teams, arts clubs, science groups and other activities?
summary:
After-school clubs give students a place to explore interests beyond regular lessons. A science group, music club, drama team or chess club can help students meet friends and practice new skills. Sports teams are also important: they give students a chance to exercise, cooperate and represent their school. These activities can make school feel more connected.

Schools have limited budgets. Equipment, coaches, instruments, room space and transport all cost money. If one activity receives much more support, students in other groups may feel ignored. Some clubs need only a small room, while a sports team may need a field and travel costs. Fairness does not always mean spending the same amount on every group.

Students and teachers could list what each activity needs and how many people it serves. A school might set a basic amount for every club, then fund extra requests based on clear reasons. How should schools divide activity budgets? Which opportunities should every student be able to try?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should schools spend more money on clubs than sports?

title: Should schools teach students how to manage money?
description: Should personal finance be a required school subject, or should families teach it at home?
summary:
Students make money choices long before they have full-time jobs. They may receive pocket money, buy snacks or save for something important. A school lesson could explain how to make a simple budget, compare prices and understand that borrowing money creates a responsibility. Students could practice with pretend examples before making real decisions.

Families have different ways of handling money, and some people may feel uncomfortable discussing their finances in class. A short course cannot prepare students for every situation. Schools also have limited time, so adding a new subject could mean less time for another important skill.

A practical course could focus on everyday choices and avoid asking students to share private details. Teachers might use fictional budgets and invite local experts to explain common terms. Should every student take a money-skills class? Which topics would be most useful, and who should decide what the class includes?

Students could practice comparing two fictional phone plans or saving toward a goal. They can discuss how a budget changes when prices or needs change.
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should schools teach students how to manage money?

title: Should schools replace some exams with projects?
description: Do projects show learning better than timed exams, or are exams a clearer way to assess individuals?
summary:
Projects give students time to research a question, make a product and explain what they learned. They can show skills that a short test may miss, such as planning, creativity and teamwork. Students who feel nervous during timed exams may be able to share their knowledge more clearly through a presentation or report.

Projects can be difficult to grade fairly. Some students have more help, devices or quiet study time at home. In a group project, one student may do most of the work. Exams let teachers check what each student can remember independently, although a test may not show every kind of understanding.

Schools could combine short individual checks with projects completed during class, where everyone has similar support. Teachers can explain grading rules before work begins. Should projects replace some exams, or should exams remain the main way to measure progress? What kind of assessment helps students learn rather than only earn a score?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should schools replace some exams with projects?

title: Should school lunch be free for every student?
description: Would free lunch for everyone make school fairer, or should support go only to families who need it?
summary:
A free lunch for every student would mean no one has to explain why they cannot pay. Students could sit together and choose a meal without worrying about different rules. Schools might also spend less time collecting payments and more time supporting students. If everyone receives the same service, there may be less embarrassment around asking for help.

Providing food for every student costs money. A school could use that money for books, staff or building repairs. Some students bring lunch from home and may not want a cafeteria meal. A targeted program may cost less and still help families who need support.

A school could ask families what they prefer and compare the cost of different plans. It might offer free meals to everyone, or provide help quietly through a simple system. Should school lunch be free for all students? How could a school make sure every student has access to food without wasting resources?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should school lunch be free for every student?

title: Should cities build more bike lanes?
description: Would more bike lanes make travel safer and cleaner, or take too much space from cars and parking?
summary:
Bike lanes can give cyclists a clearer place on busy streets. Students might feel safer riding to school, and adults could use bikes for short trips. If more people cycle, some car journeys may disappear, which can reduce traffic and make streets quieter. Bike lanes can also connect neighborhoods to parks and shops.

Building lanes can remove parking or reduce the space available to cars. A lane that starts and stops suddenly may confuse everyone. Some roads are too narrow, and people with disabilities or delivery needs may depend on vehicle access. Cities need to plan safe crossings and maintain the lanes.

A city could test a bike lane on one route and collect feedback from cyclists, drivers, businesses and people walking. It could then change the design before expanding it. Should cities create more bike lanes? Which streets would benefit, and how should planners consider people who travel in different ways?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should cities build more bike lanes?

title: Should every student learn basic cooking at school?
description: Is cooking an important life skill for all students, or should schools focus on other subjects?
summary:
A basic cooking class can help students prepare simple meals safely. They can learn to follow instructions, measure ingredients and clean a workspace. Cooking also uses math and reading in a practical way. Students may become more confident trying new foods and helping at home. A class can include recipes from different cultures.

Cooking lessons need kitchens, equipment and adult supervision. Some schools may not have enough space or money for a full course. Students have different diets, allergies and family traditions, so a recipe must be chosen carefully. Not everyone enjoys cooking, and another class might be more useful to some students.

Schools could teach a few simple recipes in a short unit and invite students to share safe, affordable ideas. They might also connect cooking to health or science lessons. Should basic cooking be part of every school program? What skills would students want to learn first?

Students could learn to read food labels, store ingredients safely and adjust a recipe for different numbers of people. These tasks connect cooking to math and health.
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should every student learn basic cooking at school?

title: Should art and music get more time in school?
description: Should schools give art and music more class time, even if that means less time for other subjects?
summary:
Art and music let students express ideas in ways that are different from essays and tests. A student may discover a talent, build confidence or learn to work patiently through a difficult piece. Creative classes can also connect to history, language and culture. Some students who struggle in other lessons may find a subject where they feel successful.

School days have limited hours. More time for art and music could mean less time for science, languages or sports. Schools also need instruments, materials and trained teachers. If a program is not planned well, students may spend time waiting for equipment rather than learning.

A school could offer short weekly lessons, after-school clubs or projects that combine arts with other subjects. It can ask students which opportunities they actually use. Should art and music receive more time? What should schools protect when they decide how to divide the timetable?

Students could also use creative work to explain a science idea or tell a local story. A shared exhibit or performance can make learning visible to families.
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should art and music get more time in school?

title: Should classes study outdoors once a week?
description: Can outdoor lessons improve learning and wellbeing, or would weather and noise make teaching harder?
summary:
An outdoor lesson can help students notice nature instead of only reading about it. A science class could observe plants or clouds, while an art class could sketch shapes and colors. Moving outside may also help students feel more awake after sitting for a long time. A nearby park or school yard can provide useful examples.

Outdoor lessons depend on weather, safe spaces and clear planning. Noise can make it hard to hear instructions, and some students may have allergies or mobility needs. A teacher cannot always bring books and equipment outside. If the class goes outdoors without a goal, students may find it difficult to focus.

Schools could start with one planned outdoor lesson each month and make sure every student can take part. Teachers can prepare a backup plan for rain. Should classes study outside more often? Which subjects would benefit, and what would make an outdoor lesson comfortable and safe?
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should classes study outdoors once a week?

title: Should museums offer free entry to students?
description: Would free museum visits help students learn, or should schools pay for visits when they are part of class?
summary:
Museums can bring history, art and science to life. Students may understand an idea better when they can see an object, experiment or artwork in person. Free entry could help families visit on their own, not only during a school trip. It may also make museums feel open to more people in the community.

Museums need money to care for collections, pay staff and create exhibits. If every student visit is free, they may need public funding or donations to cover costs. A free ticket does not solve the cost of transport, and some students live far from a museum.

A museum could offer free student days, discounted tickets or free entry when a teacher books a lesson. Local governments might help pay for visits that support school learning. Should students enter museums for free? Who should cover the cost, and what kinds of visits would be most valuable?

A school might also arrange a virtual visit when travel is impossible. Museums can provide learning materials before and after a visit so the experience continues in class.
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should museums offer free entry to students?

title: Can competitive video games count as a sport?
description: Do organized video games require enough skill and teamwork to be called a sport?
summary:
Competitive video games can require quick decisions, practice and teamwork. Players may train for hours, study strategies and communicate with teammates during a match. Organized competitions have rules, coaches and audiences. Supporters say a sport is an activity where people develop skill and compete, so gaming should be included.

Other people think sports should involve more physical movement. Sitting at a screen for a long time can affect health, and not every game encourages respectful behavior. Some competitions depend on expensive computers or fast internet, which makes it harder for all students to join.

Schools can recognize gaming clubs while also encouraging movement and healthy breaks. A team might combine strategy practice with exercise and clear screen-time limits. Should competitive gaming be called a sport? What qualities make an activity a sport, and do those qualities apply to esports?

Players need to follow rules and respect opponents, just as athletes do. A school club could discuss healthy practice habits and responsible online behavior.
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Can competitive video games count as a sport?

title: Should popular tourist places limit visitor numbers?
description: Can visitor limits protect local places, or do they unfairly reduce access and income?
summary:
Popular destinations can become crowded. Too many visitors may create litter, noise or damage to fragile places. Local residents may find it harder to travel through their own town, and nature areas may not have time to recover. A visitor limit can help protect a place and make each visit calmer.

Tourism also supports jobs in hotels, restaurants, transport and guiding. A strict limit could reduce income for local families. Some people may feel that a public beach, park or historic site should be open to everyone. If tickets are expensive, limits might favor visitors who can pay more.

A destination could use timed entry, seasonal limits or different routes to spread visitors out. Local residents should help decide which places need protection. Should popular destinations limit visitors? How can a community protect its home while welcoming people who want to learn about it?

A community can share visitor information in several languages and explain why certain places need extra care. Visitors may accept limits more easily when local residents help design them.
author: LessonCaptain
flightQuestion: Should popular tourist places limit visitor numbers?

title: Should old buildings be preserved or replaced?
description: Should cities protect historic buildings, or make room for newer buildings that serve more people?
summary:
Old buildings can tell stories about how people lived and worked in the past. They may have special designs that are difficult to recreate. Keeping them can help a neighborhood feel distinctive and give residents a connection to local history. A building can also be reused as a library, home or community space.

Older buildings may be expensive to repair and may not meet current needs. A new building could provide more homes, better access or lower energy use. Preserving every old structure is not possible, and some buildings are unsafe. Cities must decide which places have enough value to protect.

Planners can ask residents, historians and building users to discuss a site before making a decision. They might preserve the front while changing the inside, or record a building before replacing it. Should historic buildings be protected? What makes a building important enough to keep?

New buildings can sometimes include public spaces or affordable homes. A careful design may keep a familiar street while meeting current needs.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should school cafeterias buy more local food?
description: Would local food make school meals fresher and support nearby farms, or make menus more expensive?
summary:
Buying food from nearby farms can connect students with the people who grow their meals. Some ingredients may travel a shorter distance and arrive fresh. Schools can use menus to introduce seasonal foods and support local businesses. A farm visit or a short interview can make the food system easier to understand.

Local farms may not grow every ingredient a school needs. Their prices can change with the season, and a large cafeteria may need more food than one farm can supply. A menu based only on nearby products could become less varied or more expensive.

Schools might start with one local ingredient each week and compare student reactions and costs. They can keep other foods on the menu and work with several suppliers. Should cafeterias buy more local food? What matters most: freshness, price, choice or support for the local community?

Schools can explain where ingredients come from and how menus change during the year. Students may be more willing to try foods when they understand the story behind them.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should teenagers have part-time jobs during school?
description: Can a small job teach useful skills, or can work leave students with too little time to study and rest?
summary:
A part-time job can help teenagers learn to be reliable, communicate with adults and manage their own money. Students may gain experience before choosing a future career. A job can also give someone more independence and help them understand the effort behind everyday services.

Work takes time and energy. A student who works late may have less time for homework, sleep, sports or family. Some jobs are stressful, and teenagers need fair treatment and safe conditions. Not every student has the same need to earn money, so a job should not become an expectation for everyone.

Families and schools can help students plan a schedule and notice when work becomes too much. Employers can offer reasonable hours that respect school responsibilities. Should teenagers work during the school year? What limits would protect their learning, health and free time?

A job should not interfere with school attendance or safe travel home. Students can also learn about fair pay, breaks and who to contact if a problem occurs.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should schools make lunch breaks phone-free?
description: Would a phone-free lunch help students talk to each other, or take away a useful way to relax and connect?
summary:
A phone-free lunch could encourage students to talk face to face, play a game or simply notice what is happening around them. Some students say they feel pressure to check messages all day. A short break without screens may help people rest before afternoon lessons and make it easier to meet new classmates.

Phones also help students contact family, listen to music or relax alone. Some students use translation or accessibility tools. A strict rule may feel unfair if students have different needs or if adults are allowed to use their phones. Collecting devices can create extra work for school staff.

A school might offer phone-free tables instead of banning phones everywhere. Students could help set rules and explain exceptions for safety or accessibility. Should lunch be phone-free, or should students decide how to spend the break? What kind of rule would encourage connection without ignoring individual needs?

Students may want a trial period before deciding. The school can notice whether conversations change and whether students still have a safe way to reach an adult.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should students choose their own partners for projects?
description: Do students work better with friends, or should teachers create groups to ensure everyone participates?
summary:
Choosing a partner can make a project feel comfortable. Friends may know how to share ideas and divide tasks. Students can also choose someone whose skills work well with their own. When people have a choice, they may feel more responsible for the project and more willing to begin.

Students who are always chosen last may feel left out. Friends can get distracted, and a group of similar people may not consider different ideas. A teacher who creates groups can help students meet new classmates and balance skills, although students may not like every pairing.

One option is to let students choose partners sometimes and have teachers make groups at other times. A class could also use a fair rotation so everyone gets a chance to work together. Should students choose their project partners? How can a teacher make group work both comfortable and inclusive?

A project can include individual responsibilities so each person has a clear contribution. Students should also be able to ask a teacher for help if a partnership becomes difficult.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should media literacy be a required school subject?
description: Should every student learn how to check online information, or should those skills be taught across all subjects?
summary:
Students see information in videos, messages, news stories and social media posts. A media literacy class could help them ask who made a message, what evidence it uses and what it wants the audience to believe. Students could practice checking a claim before sharing it. These skills can support learning in science, history and daily life.

Schools already teach many subjects, and adding a new course may reduce time for something else. Media habits also change quickly, so teachers need resources and training. Some skills may fit better inside existing lessons, where students can check sources related to the subject they are studying.

Schools could teach a short required unit and continue practice across classes. Students can bring examples and discuss how to check them respectfully. Should media literacy be a separate subject, part of every class, or both? Which skills would help students make careful decisions online?

The goal is not to distrust every message. It is to pause, look for the original source and separate a fact from an opinion before deciding what to share.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should parks provide free sports equipment?
description: Would shared balls and games help more people use parks, or would the equipment be lost or damaged?
summary:
Free sports equipment could make parks more welcoming. People who do not own a ball, racket or skipping rope could still play. A simple lending box might help children and families try different activities without buying gear first. Shared equipment can also encourage people who arrive alone to join a game.

Equipment can get lost, broken or left in the rain. Someone needs to check it, clean it and replace unsafe items. A park may have limited space, and not every visitor wants to play sports. If the equipment is not easy to borrow, only a few people may use it.

A community could test a small lending station with sturdy equipment and clear instructions. Local groups might help care for it. Should parks offer free sports equipment? Which items would be most useful, and who should be responsible for keeping them safe?

Some people may prefer quiet activities, so sports should not take over every part of a park. A lending box can sit near an open area without blocking walking paths.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should school libraries stay open after classes?
description: Would later library hours give students a quiet place to learn, or create staffing and transport problems?
summary:
A library that stays open after school can give students a quiet place to read, finish homework or use a computer. It may help students who share a busy home or do not have internet access. Students can also join clubs or ask for help before going home.

Keeping a library open requires staff, lighting and transport plans. Some students need to go home early to care for family or attend activities. If buses stop running before the library closes, students may not be able to stay safely. A quiet space also needs clear rules so everyone can focus.

Schools could keep the library open one or two afternoons each week and ask students whether they use it. Community volunteers might support events, while school staff remain responsible for safety. Should libraries stay open after classes? What schedule would help students and work for families?

A library can offer a range of activities, from quiet reading to supervised homework help. Students should be able to choose whether to join a group or work alone.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should first aid be taught to every student?
description: Would basic first-aid lessons help students respond calmly in emergencies, or is the training too difficult to require?
summary:
Basic first-aid lessons can teach students how to stay calm, get help and respond safely when someone is hurt. A student may be the first person nearby when a classmate falls or a family member feels unwell. Learning what to do and what not to do can reduce confusion while an adult or emergency service arrives.

First aid requires accurate instruction and practice. Schools need trained teachers, supplies and time in the timetable. Students should not be expected to perform tasks beyond their training, and lessons must explain when to call an adult. Some situations can be upsetting, so teachers need to present examples carefully.

A short course could focus on simple, age-appropriate steps and be repeated every few years. Local health professionals might help teach it. Should every student take first-aid lessons? What should students learn, and how can schools make the training safe and practical?

Students can practice simple scenarios with clear instructions and no pressure to act beyond their ability. The most important first step is often to find a responsible adult.
author: LessonCaptain

title: Should every school have a quiet room?
description: Would a quiet room help students focus or take a short break, or would schools struggle to supervise and provide one?
summary:
A quiet room can give students a place to read, study or take a short break from noise. Some students find busy corridors and crowded lunch areas tiring. A calm space may help someone return to class ready to listen. It can also support students who need a quiet place to work during free time.

Schools have limited rooms, and a quiet room needs clear rules and supervision. Students may disagree about whether it is for studying, resting or meeting with a counselor. If the space is too small, not everyone can use it. Staff must also make sure the room is safe and welcoming.

A school could ask students how they would use a quiet room and set a simple sign-up system. The room might be open at certain times, with an adult nearby. Should every school provide a quiet space? What rules would make it useful for different students?
author: LessonCaptain

title: Our School Pond Journal
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Our class has a small pond near the school gate in our city. On Monday, we see green plants in the water. We also see five tiny tadpoles. Our teacher gives us a journal. We draw what we see. We do not put our hands in the pond.

On Wednesday, the water looks low. The sun is hot. We ask, “Do the tadpoles have enough water?” The teacher says we can look again tomorrow. We write the date and draw the water line. We learn that a good question needs careful looking.

On Friday, there is rain. The water line is high again. A bird drinks beside the pond. We see that the water helps more than one animal. We want to clean the area, but we leave the pond plants in place. Small animals can hide there. In our journal, we write one idea: pick up litter on the path, and let the pond stay a home for living things.
description: An original A1 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the class leave pond plants for the tadpoles?

title: Beetles in the Garden
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Mina and her class work in the school garden. They find two beetles under a leaf. One beetle is brown. One is black. The children want to know where the beetles go, so they make a simple map. Their teacher asks them to watch and draw, not to take the beetles home.

At first, the children think the beetles eat the flowers. They look again after lunch. The beetles are near old leaves on the ground. Mina writes this in her book. She learns that a first idea can be wrong. Looking twice can help.

The class puts water near the plants and takes plastic off the soil. They leave the old leaves where some little animals live. They make a sign for other students: “Please walk on the path.” On the next day, they see a worm and another beetle. Their garden is a place for plants, small animals, and people to learn together.
description: An original A1 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the children move the beetles from their garden?

title: The Family Sleep Timer
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Leo likes games on the family tablet. His sister likes to draw on it. At night, they both want one more turn. Their mother asks how they feel in the morning. Leo says he is tired at school. His sister says she is tired too.

The family makes a plan. They set a timer on the tablet. When it rings, Leo puts the game away. His sister finishes her drawing and saves it. They read a short book before bed. The first night is hard. Leo feels cross, so he tells his family. They listen and move the timer five minutes later on game night.

After a week, the children talk about the plan. They can wake up more easily. Their friends have different plans at home, and that is okay. Leo learns that a rule works best when people can explain what they need. The family keeps the timer, but they check the rule together each Sunday.
description: An original A1 reading about psychology, health, family.
flightQuestion: Should every family member use the same screen timer?

title: A Board for Neighbors
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Asha and her father live on a busy city street. Some neighbors use a phone board to share news. Asha sees a message: “Mrs Lim needs help with her shopping.” She wants to help. Her father says they should ask Mrs Lim what she needs first.

Mrs Lim says she can carry small bags, but big bags hurt her arm. Asha and her father take the big bags home with her. Mrs Lim is happy. She also says she cannot always see messages on a phone. The neighbors talk about this at their meeting.

They put a paper board in the building too. People can read a note there or use the phone board. Asha asks everyone before she shares a name or a photo. She learns that helping means listening. It also means keeping people safe and comfortable. The new plan lets more families take part, including neighbors who do not use the phone app.
description: An original A1 reading about psychology, health, family.
flightQuestion: Should the neighbors keep paper notes beside their phone board?

title: The Welcome Circle
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
A new student, Amir, joins the class on Monday. Some children want to clap and sing. Others think a quiet hello is better. Their teacher asks them to wait and ask Amir what he prefers. Amir says a big song would make him nervous, but he would like someone to show him the library.

The class starts a welcome circle. Each child may say one friendly thing or show a place in the school. Nobody has to speak in front of everyone. Amir shares a game he played at his old school. Lina says her family plays a different game at home. The children try both games at break time.

After a week, the teacher asks how the circle worked. Amir says he felt more comfortable because the class listened. The children learn that families and schools have different customs. A welcome can be warm without being loud. They write down several ways to greet the next new student and remember to ask first.
description: An original A2 reading about psychology, society, education.
flightQuestion: Should classmates ask new students how they like to be welcomed?

title: The Class Festival Library
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
The school library wants a display about celebrations. At first, the class chooses pictures of the festival most children know. Then Mei notices that several classmates celebrate other days. One student says her family has no festival this month. The teacher asks everyone to share only what they feel happy sharing.

Small groups make cards. A card can show a food, a greeting, a song, or a family activity. It does not have to speak for a whole country. Mei writes about a special meal at home and asks her grandmother to check the words. Another student draws a quiet day when his family visits relatives.

The class leaves an empty space on the shelf for more cards later. They do not ask anyone to wear a costume or answer a question if they feel shy. Visitors can read the cards and ask polite questions. The display helps the children learn that culture is made of many personal stories, not one rule for everyone.
description: An original A2 reading about psychology, society, education.
flightQuestion: Should a class display only the festivals most students know?

title: The River Bird Survey
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
The river beside Nila’s city bends around a small island. Her class wants to find out why more birds gather there in spring. They draw a map with the river bend, a footpath, trees, and a patch of reeds. Each group watches for ten minutes at the same time of day. They count birds but do not touch nests.

The first group sees only three birds. A second group sees eight after a rain shower. Their teacher warns them that one count cannot prove the reason. The class visits again, records the weather, and compares the island with a busy part of the riverbank. The reeds give insects shelter, and some birds feed on those insects.

Nila suggests closing the whole footpath. Another student thinks a short quiet section would protect the nests while letting people walk by the river. The class writes both ideas in a letter to the park team. Their map and repeated counts help them explain why this particular part of the river matters.
description: An original B1 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the class close the river path during nesting season?

title: The Night Moth Garden
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
A community garden sits between two roads in Sami’s neighborhood. His science group notices that moths visit the flowers at dusk, but few appear near the bright lamps beside the east road. They draw the garden and mark the lamps, flowers, and darker corners. Over four evenings, they count moths without catching them.

Their counts suggest a pattern, but the group knows other things may matter. The darker corner also has more flowers. They ask the gardener which plants bloom at night and learn that moths carry pollen between some flowers. The children add plant names to their map and plan a second survey.

Some neighbors want brighter lights for the path. Sami thinks the town could keep the walking path safe while dimming lamps beside the flower beds. The group presents both needs at a garden meeting. They explain how a small change in one place might help animals without leaving people in the dark. The town agrees to test the idea for a month.
description: An original B1 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the town dim garden lights to help night moths?

title: A Family Focus Experiment
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Rina uses a tablet for homework, but messages from her friends often interrupt her. Her younger brother needs the same tablet to read a school article. Their family decides to test a plan for one week instead of arguing about one strict rule.

On three evenings, Rina turns off message alerts for twenty minutes. On the other evenings, she leaves them on. She writes down when she finishes her reading and how focused she feels. Her brother records whether he can get the tablet when he needs it. Their mother reminds them that a timer cannot measure every feeling, so they talk as well as collect numbers.

Rina finishes sooner without alerts, but her brother sometimes needs to ask a question. The family creates a shared homework time and keeps one way to contact each other. Rina tells her class about the experiment. Other families describe different routines, and nobody claims that one rule must work for everyone. The lesson is to test a change, listen, and adjust it together.
description: An original B1 reading about psychology, health, education.
flightQuestion: Should Rina’s family switch off every phone during homework?

title: A Kinder Class Message Board
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
The class has an online board for homework questions. At first, students post only about lessons. Soon someone writes, “I feel worried about tomorrow’s presentation.” Several classmates answer kindly, but one message says the student should stop worrying. The teacher asks the class how a public board can support people without making them feel exposed.

They ask families for ideas and agree on simple rules. Students may share study tips, but nobody has to explain private feelings online. A worried student can ask the teacher for a quiet conversation. The board also has a link to the school support team. Before posting, students pause to think about how their words may sound to another person.

For a week, the class reads sample messages and discusses which replies show care. They learn that technology can help a group, but it cannot replace listening face to face. Their final rules protect learning, privacy, and wellbeing. Families receive a copy so they know how the board is used.
description: An original B1 reading about psychology, health, education.
flightQuestion: Should the class allow anonymous messages on its board?

title: Recipes on a Family Map
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
When her class studies local history, Maya brings a recipe from her grandfather. He first cooked the dish in a coastal town, using fish from the morning market. After the family moved inland, he used beans instead. Maya marks both places on a map and writes the dates beside them.

Other students bring food stories too. One family changed a recipe because an ingredient was expensive. Another makes the same meal only when relatives meet. The class learns that a dish can travel with people and change with the place where they live. They compare the stories with old market photographs and learn why a new road changed what the town could buy.

The teacher asks before putting any recipe online. Some families are happy to share; others want to keep a detail private. Maya includes only the parts her grandfather approves. Their class map shows movement, trade, and family choices. It also shows that no single recipe represents everyone from one place.
description: An original B1 reading about food, culture, history.
flightQuestion: Should the class put family recipes on a public map?

title: The Market Supper Project
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Tariq’s class plans a supper for families at the city hall. Before choosing dishes, they visit the market with a map. A seller explains that fruit once came by boat from the river, while trucks now bring it from farms farther away. An older neighbor remembers when the market opened only twice a week.

Students ask relatives what they like to cook and what they can afford. One family brings a dish from a different region. Another asks for a meal without nuts. The class realizes that a shared table needs clear labels and several choices. They write short cards explaining where ingredients came from and how recipes changed over time.

Some students argue that every dish should use local food. Tariq points out that the city’s own history includes travel and trade. The group chooses a mix of nearby produce and family recipes from other places. At the supper, guests talk about memories and new tastes. The project turns a meal into a map of people, places, and change.
description: An original B1 reading about food, culture, history.
flightQuestion: Should the supper use only foods grown near the town?

title: The Wetland beside the Station
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Behind the city’s railway station lies a narrow wetland that many passengers barely notice. When plans for a longer platform appear, Isha’s class decides to investigate what lives there before offering an opinion. They divide the area into sections on a map, measure water depth after rain, and count the birds they can identify from a distance.

The students find frogs in the shallows and dragonfly larvae in the water. Their teacher explains that these animals depend on connected habitats: a dry path, reeds, and pools that remain wet long enough for young animals to develop. The wetland also absorbs some heavy rain, although the class cannot measure exactly how much flooding it prevents.

Rail passengers need safe access, and the town may need a longer platform. The class proposes a survey by professional ecologists before any work begins. They suggest comparing alternative platform shapes and recording wildlife through different seasons. Their evidence cannot settle the decision alone, but it makes the hidden wetland visible to the people who will decide its future.
description: An original B2 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the station extend its platform into the wetland?

title: Coral Watch on the Island
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
The island reef attracts visitors, but its coral has become pale after a period of unusually warm water. A school science club joins a local guide to observe the reef from marked places. They record water temperature, photograph the same small area each week, and note where fish are still feeding. The guide warns them that a few photographs cannot reveal the whole reef’s health.

Coral is made by living animals, and the structures they build provide shelter for many species. Their location matters: the sheltered side of the island has calmer water than the exposed side, so the two areas may change differently. The club plots both sites on a map instead of treating the reef as one uniform place.

Some residents earn money by guiding visitors, while others want the reef closed until it recovers. The students discuss limited visits on fixed routes, with a review after several months. They present their observations as evidence, not a final verdict. Protecting the habitat and supporting families both matter in the island’s decision.
description: An original B2 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should visitors avoid the reef while its coral recovers?

title: Designing an App Everyone Can Use
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
A school plans an app for homework notices and wellbeing resources. The first design looks attractive, but a student called Noor discovers that her grandmother cannot read the small text when she helps with homework. Another family shares one phone, so alerts arrive at a time when nobody can check them.

Instead of assuming the app will work for everyone, the student design team interviews families. They ask about text size, language, internet access, and whether private support messages should appear on a shared screen. The answers reveal practical barriers as well as feelings: some people worry they will miss important information or expose a personal problem.

The team makes the text larger, adds a paper notice option, and separates private wellbeing contacts from public class updates. They test the revised design with the same families and record what still fails. The principal wants to launch quickly, but the students argue for another round of testing. A useful school tool should help people learn without making some families invisible.
description: An original B2 reading about psychology, health, education.
flightQuestion: Should the school launch its app before every family can use it?

title: The Class Sleep Study
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
After a week of tired mornings, a class asks whether late screen use affects concentration. Their teacher suggests a voluntary study, but insists that students must never feel pressured to share private routines. Families can choose to keep a simple diary at home, recording bedtime and how alert a child feels the next morning.

The class discusses what the diary can and cannot show. A child might sleep poorly because of noise, illness, or worry rather than a phone. The group compares anonymous patterns, not named students, and avoids claiming that a single week proves a cause. They also ask whether homework deadlines make it difficult to put devices away early.

Some pupils want a school rule banning screens after dinner. Others point out that families have different schedules and may use a device for reading or contacting relatives. The class recommends clearer homework times and optional screen reminders. The study teaches them to protect privacy, question simple explanations, and design health advice that people can actually follow.
description: An original B2 reading about psychology, health, education.
flightQuestion: Should the class publish every student’s sleep results?

title: A Meal across Three Places
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Leila’s family recipe began near a mountain village, travelled to a port, and changed again when her grandparents moved to a city. She traces those places on a map for a local museum project. The earliest version used a grain grown near the village. At the port, cooks added a spice brought by traders. In the city, her grandmother changed the cooking time to fit a small apartment kitchen.

The museum wants a display called “Traditional Food.” Leila wonders which version would deserve that label. Her grandfather says the changes are part of the family’s history, not mistakes. She interviews relatives, checks the dates against old photographs, and records where each ingredient came from. She also asks permission before sharing a family story publicly.

The final display shows three recipe cards connected by a route, rather than claiming that one dish has a single fixed form. Visitors can see how geography, trade, and household needs shape culture. Leila hopes the exhibit invites other families to tell their own food stories without pretending that one family speaks for a whole community.
description: An original B2 reading about food, culture, history.
flightQuestion: Should a museum label one family dish as traditional?

title: Whose Market History?
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
A city plans to rebuild its market beside a new bus route. Some officials call the old stalls inconvenient, while long-time sellers describe them as part of the city’s identity. Jae’s class creates a history project to understand the disagreement. They map where the river, bus stop, and food stalls stood in three different decades.

Interviews reveal that families used the market for more than shopping. People exchanged recipes, found seasonal produce, and met relatives after work. Yet the old layout is difficult for some wheelchair users, and sellers need safer storage. The class does not treat every memory as proof that nothing should change. It compares memories with photographs and asks whose stories have been left out.

Jae suggests keeping a few stalls while redesigning the paths and adding a display about the market’s changing food culture. Other students prefer a completely new building. Their report presents both options, the costs they could identify, and questions still unanswered. The town’s decision will affect trade and daily life, so more than one generation deserves a voice.
description: An original B2 reading about food, culture, history.
flightQuestion: Should the town preserve stalls from its old market?

title: Birds beside the River Path
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Our town has a path by the river. Many people walk there. Birds live in the reeds near the water. A school group wants to learn about the birds. We draw a simple map. We mark the path, the reeds, and a small bridge.

On Monday, we count four birds near the bridge. On Tuesday, we count seven birds near the reeds. We go at the same time each day. Our teacher says one count is not enough. We need to look again before we give advice.

We also see a plastic bag in the water. We ask an adult to help remove it safely. We do not go into the river or touch the birds. The reeds are a home for small animals, so we leave them there. At the end of the week, we show our map to the town. We ask for a bin beside the path and a quiet place near the reeds. People can enjoy the river while animals have space too.
description: An original A1 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the town keep a quiet path for river birds?

title: Bees near Our School
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
There are flowers behind our school. Small bees visit them in the morning. Our class makes a map of the garden. We mark the flowers, a wall, and a road. The road is noisy, but the garden is quiet.

We want to know which flowers bees visit. For ten minutes, we watch from the path. We do not catch a bee. We write the number of bees in our books. We look again the next day. More bees come when the sun is warm. Our teacher says the weather may change our count.

The school wants to cut all the flowers and make a new path. Some students want a path, but they also want to help the bees. We ask if the path can go beside the wall instead. Then the flowers can stay. The school asks the gardener to look at our map. We learn that a small place can be important for animals and people.
description: An original A1 reading about science, animals, biology.
flightQuestion: Should the school leave flowers for the bees?

title: My Phone and My Sleep
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Nara reads messages on her phone at night. She goes to bed late and feels tired at school. Her family asks how they can help. Nara says she needs the phone for homework, but she also wants to talk with friends.

For one week, Nara writes a sleep diary. She writes when she puts the phone down and how she feels in the morning. Her teacher says the diary is private. Nara may talk about it with her family, but she does not have to show it to the class.

After three days, Nara tries a new plan. She checks messages before homework, then turns off the sound. At nine, she puts the phone on a table outside her room. She sleeps earlier on most nights. One night is different because the street is loud. Nara learns that a phone is not the only reason for poor sleep. Her family keeps talking and changes the plan when it does not work.
description: An original A1 reading about psychology, health, education.
flightQuestion: Should Nara put her phone away before homework ends?

title: A Message for the Building
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Omar and his mother live in a large city building. The people there have a phone group. One day, a neighbor asks for help. She cannot carry food upstairs because her leg hurts. Omar wants to post her name and room number. His mother says they must ask the neighbor first.

The neighbor says yes to help, but no to a public photo. Omar carries one bag. His mother carries another. Later, they learn that some older people in the building do not use the phone group. At a meeting, Omar suggests a paper board near the door.

The neighbors agree. A person can choose to put a note on the paper board, send a phone message, or ask for help in person. Omar’s school class talks about the plan. They say a good tool should help many people and protect private information. Omar feels proud because he listened before he shared. His family now checks both boards each week.
description: An original A1 reading about psychology, health, education.
flightQuestion: Should the building share help requests on paper too?

title: Food on Our City Map
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Lia’s class makes a map of food in their city. First, they mark a market near the river. Then they mark a new shop by the bus station. Lia asks her grandfather about the old market. He says people came by boat to sell fruit many years ago. Now trucks bring fruit by road.

Lia’s family buys rice and vegetables at the market. Her friend’s family cooks a different meal with the same vegetables. The class learns that one food can be part of many family traditions. They ask before they write anyone’s recipe on the map.

At school, each student adds one place and one short story. The map shows old and new roads, shops, and homes. It does not say that every family in the city eats the same food. Lia puts her grandfather’s boat story beside the river. Her friend adds a recipe note by the bus station. Their map helps people see how places and daily meals change over time.
description: An original A1 reading about food, culture, history.
flightQuestion: Should a city food map include family stories?

title: Grandma’s Market Recipe
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Mina helps her grandmother cook on Saturday. They go to the market together. Grandma tells Mina that she made this dish in another town when she was young. On a map, she shows Mina the town and the road she took to move here.

One food in the old recipe is hard to buy in their new town. Grandma now uses a local vegetable. Mina asks, “Is it still the same family dish?” Grandma smiles and says that families can keep a story even when a meal changes.

Mina writes the recipe in a notebook. She writes both the old food and the new one. She asks Grandma if she can share the page at school. Grandma says yes, but she wants Mina to tell the travel story too. At school, friends talk about meals from their homes. Some foods are new to Mina. She learns that every family has its own way of cooking and remembering. The market connects many people and places.
description: An original A1 reading about food, culture, history.
flightQuestion: Should Mina change her grandmother’s recipe for local food?

title: A Map for the Family Visit
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Ella’s family plans to visit her grandmother across the city. The fastest route uses a new road, but Grandma asks to pass through her old neighborhood. Ella opens a map and finds two possible journeys. The old route takes twenty minutes longer and crosses a busy bridge.

Grandma shows Ella where she went to school and where her family lived. Some buildings have disappeared, but the river and a small park are still there. Ella marks the places on the map. Her brother wants to arrive early so they can cook lunch together. The family talks about how much time they have.

They decide to take the old route on the way there and the fast road on the way home. Grandma tells one story at each stop, and Ella records the stories only after asking permission. The trip is not just about reaching a house. The map helps the family connect places with memories, while their plan respects everyone’s time.
description: An original A2 reading about family, geography, cities.
flightQuestion: Should the family choose the longer route past Grandma’s old home?

title: A Walk with Three Generations
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Three generations of Jo’s family want to walk to the river market in their city. Jo chooses the shortest route on a phone map, but her grandfather points out that it has no shade. Her younger cousin finds a second route through a park. It is longer, yet it has benches and a safe crossing.

The family checks the weather and talks about what everyone needs. Grandfather can walk well if they stop once. The cousin wants to see the pond in the park. Jo marks the market, the park, and both crossings on a simple map. She also checks when the market closes.

They choose the park route and leave a little earlier. On the way, Grandfather tells Jo that the river used to follow a different path before the road was built. Jo adds this story to a family travel note. She learns that a good route is more than a short line between two places. People’s ages, memories, and comfort can change the best choice.
description: An original A2 reading about family, geography, cities.
flightQuestion: Should the family take the shaded route even if it is longer?

title: A Family Agreement for the Coast
author: LessonCaptain
summary:
Every summer, Ravi’s extended family visits the same stretch of coast. They picnic near the dunes and remember the afternoons their grandparents spent there. This year, a conservation group asks visitors to avoid part of the beach because birds are nesting among the grass. Some relatives worry that the new signs will end a family tradition.

Ravi walks with a local guide and learns that the birds choose sheltered sand where people rarely pass. A single visit may seem harmless, but repeated footsteps can damage the plants that hold the dunes in place.
